utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen. Yes, I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Oric, you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, also good morning to my learned friends from the Defence. I am here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Wubben, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Vasvija Vidovic, and together with Mr. John Jones I appear for Mr. Naser Oric. We have with us here our legal assistant, Ms. Jasmina Cosic, and our CaseMap manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Vidovic, and good morning to you and your team. First of all, my apologies for starting a few minutes late. The reason mainly was that I had a meeting scheduled for this morning that went a little bit beyond the time. So let's see whether there are any preliminaries? MR. DI FAZIO: One submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. If Your Honours please, we filed the declaration on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And there are some annexes attached to it. The Prosecution has an application to make that those annexes be placed under seal for various reasons. I can explain the reasons to you. It will only take me a minute or so, and I think I'd prefer to do that in closed session. It shouldn't take very long at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Di Fazio. Let's go into private session, not closed session, for a while. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones or Madam Vidovic, is there going to be a reaction on this filing today on your part or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We will file a response to this submission, but I'm not sure whether we can do it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or rather we will do it in the course of this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is more or less acceptable with us, provided we don't prolong this matter unduly. So, any further preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just one small one. The week before last we indicated that we objected to the authenticity of certain Prosecution exhibits and I don't think we mentioned which ones. It was P590 and P591, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, while we are on this question of challenged documents, please try -- as we approach the end of the case, please try, both sides, to make out a list of the documents that you are challenging so that we will eventually compare it with our own and make sure that we are not missing any documents, the challenge of which is being made by either of you. All right. We keep -- we keep a list, but it may happen sometimes that there is a mistake, one of the documents may not be accounted for or something like that. All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just in that regard, Your Honour, we did consider the possibility of having a separate filing at some point on authenticity in which we would attach some sort of a table or annex, but in which we might also have a summary of the nature of the objection. That way, also, given that we have a limited number of pages for the post-trial brief, we wouldn't take up an excessive amount of space --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Jones. That would be extremely helpful, Mr. Jones, also because, I think I may have told you this sometime before, but the system that I work with and which I will be suggesting to my colleagues is that when the case hearing and submissions are over and we start with our deliberations, the very first thing that I would be proposing to do is to sit down for as long as necessary and go through each and over one of the documents that are challenged, either individually -- individually, but also if they belong to a class or a category. And that will be the first decision that we will take before we proceed any further. We will decide on which documents are being admitted for the purpose of our deliberations and which are being excluded. All right. So it will be important for us to know with the utmost precision possible that we are examining and deciding on each and every single document that has been challenged, the authenticity of which has been challenged. All right. Thank you. In Brdjanin it took us almost two weeks to do that exercise -- no, sorry, about a week, a week and a few days. And the number of documents wasn't as -- challenged documents wasn't as big as it is in this case. So can we bring in the witness, Madam Usher, please? I understand that you have decided not to call the second witness you had for this week, who was scheduled to testify on Thursday and Friday. On Thursday it's not a problem in the least because, as I told you before, I have plenary in which we elect the new President and the new Vice-President, and that is bound to be followed by a few meetings because there will be also the redistribution or recomposition of Chambers, our selection of Presidents of Chambers. So it's going to be quite a long and busy day, quite a long and busy day. So we are not going to miss that. If there are any leftovers with this witness, we will obviously go to Friday. It is also possible to continue on Thursday afternoon; however, I'm advised that the -- at least two hours are needed to put back the strangers' gallery in order to receive -- receive visitors because the plenary meeting will take place over there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, officer, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. Welcome to this Tribunal. I am the Presiding Judge. My name is Carmel Agius, and I come from Malta. To my right I'm flanked by Judge Hans Hendrik Brydensholt from the Kingdom of Denmark, and on my left I have Judge Professor Albert Eser from Germany. Together we compose this Trial Chamber that is conducting the trial against Naser Oric. You have been summoned here as a Defence witness and very soon you will start with your testimony. Our Rules require that before you do so in lieu of an oath which you would have in your own jurisdiction you make a solemn declaration which is contained in a piece of paper that is going to be handed to you now. That is equivalent to an oath. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. The procedure here is pretty much like at home, like the one you're used to. Since you've been summoned by the Defence, it will be the Defence, Mr. Jones I take it, who will go first with his direct examination of you. And then he will be followed by the lead counsel of the team of the Prosecution, in this case Mr. Jan Wubben. After that there will be a re-examination, and, finally, if at all, some questions from the Bench. Mr. Jones, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And good morning from me.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, could you please give the Court your full name.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Captain David Lawrence MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just so you know, I'm going to be leaving a small pause for interpretation, just for your information. Please confirm, if you can, the following details: You were born on the 27th of September, 1963, in Hamilton, Ontario, in Canada?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And that you're Canadian by nationality.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you trained as a field artillery officer, specialising in anti-aircraft defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, is it right that you've spent 17 and a half years in the Canadian forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you've been an instructor in the Canadian forces for eight years on over 50 courses?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you tell us firstly in what subjects you were an instructor? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I predominantly started out as an air defence instructor, I have a specialty course in that, but in the last three years I have specialised in peacekeeping training, specifically military observer training, at the Canadian forces peace support training centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as far as your training to be an artillery instructor is concerned, is it right that you attended a year-long air defence instructor and gunnery course at the Canadian air defence artillery school from July 1993 to June 1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it correct that you have had four overseas postings, in Germany, in the former Yugoslavia as a UN military observer, in the United States as an exchange instructor, and in Sierra Leone as a military observer?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, as a field artillery officer, are you familiar with a wide range of artillery weapons, their calibres, their ranges, and other characteristics?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, we've studied that as -- in our basic training to become an artillery officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, were you deployed to a Bosnia and Herzegovina as a United Nations military observer, or UNMO, on the 28th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was your rank at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you spend two weeks in Zagreb and then five and a half months in Karlovac, in Croatia, as an UNMO before being deployed to Sarajevo in mid-November 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you go to Srebrenica sometime in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what dates, precisely?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I went into Srebrenica on the 27th of March, and left on the 4th of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in general terms what was the mission of UNMOs in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: The mission of a military observer is to observe and report and -- and then investigate as required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but let's go into private session for a minute or so. I just want to clear something with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed, Your Honour, and I have deliberately avoided or plan to avoid extracting any names of persons -- personnel during the course of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Be careful, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, and I will save the letter which was referred to, just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were UNMOs armed or not when they're on mission?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No, military observers are unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then why is that?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, it's been proven over the years that as a observer that's unarmed you're not a threat to the different warring parties and so the UN has said that you will be unarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you were in Sarajevo, among other things did you count artillery rounds being fired into the town of Sarajevo by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we counted the artillery rounds any time there was something shooting or firing. We would consider that a cease-fire violation, although in most cases there was no cease-fire while I was there, but that was something that we tracked all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance we have a new exhibit which we'll distribute. We distributed a copy to the Prosecution already this morning. And just for the record, this is a document headed "United Nations UNPROFOR UNMO," and dated 16 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you know who the author is of this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm the author of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you indeed write it on the 16th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, is this document -- are you going to propose that this document be filed under seal? Because if not, we'll put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wasn't proposing to, Your Honour, it's not marked as confidential and I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we can put a copy of it on the ELMO, Madam Registrar, for the public to be able to follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'll just try and anticipate one matter. You told us that you went to Srebrenica for the 27th of March, 1993, until, I think you said, the 4th of April. In this document the reference is to the 12th of April, that's in line 23, for the record, and to the 28th of April, line 26, in relation to Srebrenica. Is that correct or should those references be 12th of March and 28th of March?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: It should say 12th of March and 27th of March. It's a type error.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'm going to start with this document in relation to your tasks in Sarajevo, and I'm just going to read one short extract. "I'm writing to tell you how things went as a United Nations military observer in former Yugoslavia as it has been quite an experience. As you may have heard, I was wounded in an attack on the 3rd of April. As far as I know it hit the world news within minutes, including my name. I arrived in former Yugoslavia on 28th of May, 1992." And then I'm skipping down a few lines. "For nearly four months I was in Sarajevo as a sub-sector commander. I was inside the city and we were subject to all the same danger as the local population, maybe even more. In Sarajevo our main task was to count the incoming rounds and the few outgoing ones. We considered upwards of a thousand rounds to be an average day. When things got rough, we would call the shot so that our fellow UNMOs could take cover in their bunker." Is that correct that you were counting incoming rounds, that is rounds fired by the Serbs into Sarajevo for some four months?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during that time, you counted many thousands of rounds?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I'll ask for an exhibit number now for this document although I'm going to keep using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and Madam Registrar, the next number is D --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D894, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 894. So this document which is dated the 16th of May, 1993, and consists of two pages, the paternity of which the witness has assumed is being tendered, marked as Defence Exhibit D894.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, did you see the effect of those rounds hitting buildings in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, we did on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was one of those effects to start fires in buildings?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how frequently did that occur?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Pretty much on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with tracer fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you explain for us what that is, what tracer ammunition, what tracer fire is?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Tracer ammunition is designed to mark a target or to aid somebody in showing another soldier where they're firing. Tracer ammunition can be particular -- mostly with anti-aircraft ammunition but it can also be put into any rifle for a commander to shoot and then everybody else can see whether where he's firing. And tracer ammunition burns as it goes through the air so it's basically on fire. It's a bullet that's on fire, essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was tracer fire used by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Tracer ammunition was used all the time and normally when you fire tracer ammunition it would be four bullets and then the fifth one would be a tracer round. So you would have every fifth round tracer, and you see them going through the air. And at night-time, of course, they light up the sky. An example would be if you think back to the Persian Gulf War over Baghdad you see those rounds going through the air, that's tracers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can tracer fire cause fires in buildings?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I would say almost always if there's a fuel for it to catch on, it can be carpet or curtains on the windows or furniture or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Are you familiar with white phosphorus?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you explain for us, please, its properties and its use.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: White phosphorus is used in artillery rounds for smoke. It produces large, white cloud of smoke. When that round explodes and the white phosphorus is -- comes into contact with oxygen, with the air, it burns extremely, extremely hot, and it will set things on fire. And I've seen fires before set by white phosphorus, even in training.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And shrapnel, just simple shrapnel, can that also start fires in buildings?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: A piece of shrapnel could start a fire. When the round explodes, a lot of the shrapnel will actually, because of the explosive charge, turn white hot. And if it, again, catches something that can fuel a fire, then it will set fire to curtains, carpet, whatever, grass.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally on this subject, can you please explain for us what a delayed fuse is.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: On an artillery round, the normal fuse is designed to set off as soon as it touches something hard. A delayed fuse would have a, I'll say, a one-second delay so that that round can actually go into the ground and they're designed to produce casualties underground. So if you're dug in in bunkers or trenches, it will destroy the bunkers or trenches, whereas the non-delay fuse is designed to kill people in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right then that delayed fuses have a greater destructive power than an ordinary fuse?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: A delayed fuse round would go in the ground two or three feet and then explode and leave a much bigger hole in the ground, whereas a fuse without a delay, you may not see a lot of the effect on the ground because most of the shrapnel has been sent flying through the air, designed to kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did the Bosnian Serbs use delayed fuses?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I've seen all fuses used in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, during your training in Canada, did you ever come across fires being started simply by the use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. During the -- my training while we were firing down range, quite often if the fire index was very high the grass would catch fire, and on a number of occasions I had to go down range and put out fires that were caused by our own artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, when you were counting rounds in Sarajevo, could you actually tell what type of artillery piece was firing, what calibre and what type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Initially when I got to Sarajevo or even when I had been in Croatia earlier, I only knew the types of weapons systems that were being used during the conflict, but after -- after thousands of rounds you learn what the sound of the round going through the air is, the sound of the explosion. You might be able to see the round going through the air, the effect of the round as it -- once it lands, if you go to do an investigation on that spot. So after a couple of weeks you became very good at estimating what type of weapon had fired that round. As well, we had military observers watching in some cases the rounds being fired from the guns. So, yes, we could determine what types of rounds they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you - and, again, still sticking with when you were in Sarajevo - based on your observations conclude not just the direction from which an artillery piece was firing but also the approximate location from which shells had been fired?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, particularly as an artillery officer I'm trained in crater analysis and I can initially determine the direction of fire that that round came from. And then based on that information and further investigation, knowing the range of that type of weapon I can determine the maximum range, where that gun could have fired that round, and then I do basically a calculation on a map and I can get a rough idea where the guns were that were fired and we're trained for that for counter-battery fire where we may have to shoot back, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And even without sophisticated techniques of crater analysis, could you tell based, say, just on seeing the flashes of fire from a weapon, determine the location of that weapon?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, we knew where a lot of the guns were and on many occasions from my observations posts in Sarajevo I could actually see the guns Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. firing and you could see the flash from the muzzle, the barrel of the gun, as it fired, watch the round go through the air, and then watch it land wherever it landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in short, it's perfectly possible to know with respect to an artillery piece which is firing not just the direction from which it's shooting but actually the location. Would that be a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to your report, which is now D894, we see about half way down the following. "After Sarajevo I went to northern Bosnia on the Serbia side, actually living in Serbia." Now, was that a new posting from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I was actually being posted to Tuzla, but because of confrontation lines and crossing areas where we could safely cross, they were limited. I had to go to the team that was responsible for the crossing site near the Zvornik bridge and wait there until a crossing could be made. And then I ended up staying there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that in March 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, your report refers to you arriving at Zvornik bridge. Did you travel from Sarajevo -- in fact, from Pale to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. The normal procedure would be I guess a shuttle, if you would, and I was shuttled from Sarajevo to Kiseljak, Kiseljak to Pale, and then somebody from that team took me to the Zvornik bridge area, where I would have been shuttled then to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now I'm going to ask you to look at a new exhibit, which will be a map, and which we'll have copies distributed. And I'm going to ask also if the witness could mark the map with a highlighter. Thank you. Now, I'm going to ask you, Captain MacDonald, if you can mark several locations on this map, starting firstly with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And now Pale?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then Tuzla, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, if you keep that map with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll still ask just for now to have an exhibit number before I forget, which would be D895, I believe?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This map which is being tendered by the Defence is being entered, marked as Defence Exhibit D895.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see anything of military interest on the map to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. On the way to Zvornik on the 12th of March, as I got closer to Zvornik I had noticed that the trees and the brush had been cleared away from the road, and there was like log -- these log bunkers at regular intervals along the road. And I'd asked -- the military observer that was driving me to Zvornik had been along that road before, and he told me they were Bosnian Serb bunkers that were being used to observe that road because there was Bosnians trying to cross from the Srebrenica pocket to Tuzla and they were using that to -- or they could basically cover that road with machine-gun fire to kill anybody that was trying to cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And as you were travelling along this road to Zvornik, were these bunkers on the left-hand side or on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: They were on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So they were facing the direction of the Srebrenica pocket?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Eser would like the witness to indicate, if possible, on this map or on some other map that may be made available which road he took.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to ask if the witness could first mark with a highlighter where he saw these bunkers and then, if he can, indicate the route he took to Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's perfect, and if he could do that on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Judge Eser.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And are you marking -- perhaps, actually, to make it clear with a pen, to make it clear where you saw all these bunkers.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. So that's essentially between Caparde, or close to Caparde, and then going down towards Sekovici, that stretch of the road? Sorry, I was just looking on the map.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how were these bunkers spaced, how far apart were they?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: The bunkers were separated by what I would call line of sight. So one bunker, based on the terrain, would be able to see the other bunker. So in that case they were separated fairly evenly, but the aim that they could cover the entire road with all the bunkers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And this military observe who told you about these bunkers, had he travelled that road frequently or just a few times? Do you recall how familiar he was with that stretch of road?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: He was operating out of Pale, and he had travelled up to Zvornik on a number of occasions. But I wouldn't have that exact number, but that was his area of operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, in your report it states that you went to the Zvornik bridge area and were actually living in Serbia. What was the actual name of the village or town where you were staying?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I was living in Banja Koviljaca, or -- it was close to Loznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you mark those two locations on the map, please, Loznica and Banja Koviljaca.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you were there, did you meet a team leader from the same sector as you?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I met the team leader for that Banja Koviljaca team. We had worked together in Croatia for the five and a half months earlier in 1992. He was from Russia. I hadn't seen him since, and on the 12th of March I seen him for the first time and he was the team leader for that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Alex Vassiliev.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did he request you to join his team?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. I was on the way to Tuzla, as I mentioned earlier, and -- because we had been very good friends he asked me to stay at his team as his second in command. And I told him that I would be more than happy to stay there if the senior military observer in Tuzla agreed. He said he would phone him the next day, which he did. And the senior military observer said, yes, I could stay at that team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could -- Alex Vassiliev, could he speak Serbo-Croatian or understand it?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, he understand Serbo-Croatian at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did he tell you about a place called Konjevic Polje and what had happened there on the 12th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. On the -- on that day that I arrived, I went right to the hotel, the military observer headquarters in Banja Koviljaca. And that was the day that General Morillon was trying to -- and successfully did get into Srebrenica. However, part of the group which consisted of military observers and some British protection force troops were stopped in Konjevic Polje. Eventually that evening they did get back. They were held, they were released. They came back to the hotel -- that's actually when I seen Alex for the first time and that's when he recounted the story of what happened to them in Banja Koviljaca -- or Konjevic Polje, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what had in fact happened in Konjevic Polje on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That day the Bosnian Serb forces were pushing to squeeze the Srebrenica pocket smaller. And the women and children essentially held the -- that UN force hostage, if you would, by blocking the vehicles from moving forward or moving backwards. So all the women sat around the vehicles. They even laid their babies in front of the tires, front and back, so they couldn't drive away. And then they were holding there. And they believed that if the UN was there, that the Serb forces, the Bosnian Serb forces, would not attack. In actual fact, they did attack and they walked mortars in on the military observers' vehicle. When I say "walked them in," they slowly fired and then adjusted with very small adjustments so they wouldn't actually have rounds land on top of the vehicles. And then when one vehicle -- or one of the mortar rounds landed within a few metres of the one of the front of one of the military observer Jeeps, and we were driving soft-skinned vehicles with no armour protection. At that point they killed what was believed to be hundreds of women and children in the crowd, and the military observers at that point were able to get out of the vehicles and take cover behind some buildings. So that was part of the story that he recounted to me that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as a result of those events, did you -- did your team try to get into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, General Morillon got in that day, and we spent the next two weeks trying to get into Srebrenica. And it wasn't until the 27th of March that we were finally led into the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you actually patrolling during those two weeks? Were you actually moving around the area?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. That's another one of the military observers' main tasks. So that you can observe you conduct daily vehicle patrols, maybe even foot patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you operating just on the Serbian side of the Drina or on both sides?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I actually operated on both sides of the Drina River between Loznica and Ljubovija on the Serbian side, and between Zvornik bridge and Bratunac on the Bosnian Serb side, and also up to Caparde where we had the crossing site to go to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during that time, were you trying to establish radio contact with people in the Srebrenica pocket?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, because it was important to we tried to get information on what was going on, as there were other military observers with General Morillon in Srebrenica. So we tried to get in daily radio communications to -- just to find out what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you able to make radio contact?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: We had a very difficult time making radio contact with those in Srebrenica due to the fact that the range of the radios that we had was very limited and there were no repeater stations in that area, and, due to the terrain, the sheer rock walls and mountains in the Drina Valley, for us to get communications with Srebrenica, we had to actually get down very, very close to Srebrenica so we could talk on our radios. And so if we couldn't do that, then we had a very difficult time talking to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: While you were moving around on the Serb side of the Drina, did you see any military vehicles of any description?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw military vehicles on a regular basis, police or -- well, civilian police as well as military police vehicles. But particularly in Ljubovija one day I got there and I saw military convoys coming from the east heading, basically, down the road towards the Drina River and Bosnia. They were loaded with ammunition. They were ammunition trucks, essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you could mark on the map where that was and the direction where the vehicles were travelling.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So I see you've marked as an approximate arrow. Is that to indicate that they were travelling -- these trucks were travelling towards Bosnia and towards Bratunac, in fact?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see any artillery placements on the Serbian side of the Drina during that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. On that day I saw artillery Howitzers, artillery guns, and tanks along the bank of the Drina River on the Serbian side. And they were pointed towards Bosnia, as I turned up the road towards the town of Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And again, if you could just indicate on the map where you saw the artillery placements.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that's on the Serbian side of the Drina, south of Ljubovija. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. There was a big, open area along the river there and they were dug-in in that location, that vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what does that indicate if artillery is dug-in?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: If artillery or tanks are dug-in it is to protect them. So you want to get below ground so if you're fired on by enemy artillery, that you have some protection, because even tanks and guns and of course the personnel are vulnerable, so you want to dig-in.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And does it indicate that the artillery has either been or is intended to be in that position for some time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it would -- of course, if you're going to be there for a long time, you want to dig-in for your protection. But if you have the time, you would always dig-in. But, correct, I would assume long term, and that's what we would do in my military.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you actually see those weapons firing?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. As we came down the road from the Zvornik direction and just as we were about to turn up into Ljubovija, I saw one of the artillery guns firing. And you can see the movement because the barrel actually is on a spring, so it doesn't destroy itself, and of course you can see the flash from the muzzle, and it was firing in the direction of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about where, precisely, it was firing, where in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, it was firing in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose that is precisely what you wanted to suggest, Mr. Wubben? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you recall when that was? Obviously it's in this two-week period, but if you can be more specific.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: It would have been between the 20th to the 27th of March. I forget the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, if the witness could please be shown Defence Exhibit D879, and for the record this is a Bratunac light Infantry Brigade command dated 24 January 1993, very urgent to Drina Corps command. It says: "In accordance with a verbal order and with regard to a report submitted on the means of support for the units of the Zvornik and Bratunac Brigades," and there's a list of ammunition and units.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I wonder if you could just take your time to peruse this document, and then I'll draw your attention to paragraph 5, "the following units have arrived in the area between Loznica and Ljubovija." And then we have the list which you see before you. And numbers 1 to 4 refer to ammunition for various artillery weapons, tanks, and Howitzers, et cetera. Now, firstly, is this the approximate area, the same area, that you -- where you saw artillery, namely in the Loznica to Ljubovija area, that approximate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There was other emplacements that we saw, particularly between Loznica and Zvornik bridge, as I drove that quite often, and then the stuff -- the artillery and tanks that I had seen in Ljubovija.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you spoke earlier about the sort of damage that artillery shells and ammunition could do to buildings. You did mention tanks. What sort of damage did tanks do to property?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: A tank round is actually designed to kill another tank, and if you fire a tank round at a building it will put a hole in it. We had tank rounds fired at our buildings in Sarajevo, so I investigated this on a number of times. And a tank round might put a hole in your building two or three square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would that also have the potential to start a fire in a building?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible for a tank round also to start a fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask you just to cast your eye down this list and say which of this weaponry you saw when you were on the Serbian side of the Drina in March 1993.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I saw the -- I saw 122-millimetre artillery Howitzers, tanks, and also anti-aircraft guns, machine-guns, the three- and the four-barrel type.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. There are references to batteries here, for example, 122-millimetre, M-38 Howitzer battery. Can you explain for us what a battery consists of.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: A battery is a group of guns, normally six -- six to eight guns would be found in one battery of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm finished with that exhibit. We have a new exhibit to be distributed which the ERN is 04273565. Just while it's being distributed it's Drina Corps command, January 24 1993, very urgent to VRS headquarters. And it's signed by commander Milenko Zivanovic. "We hereby submit to you the report you submitted on VRS RS army reserves. In the area from Loznica to Ljubovija the following units are deployed."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you may notice that the list of forces, weapons, and ammunition matches almost precisely what we saw in the previous document. I don't know if, just casting your eye down that list, whether you would agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree it's very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, the previous document referred to a military police company in the Mali Zvornik area. In this document we see a reference to SVP, Independent Military Police in M-Zvornik. Did you see military police in the Zvornik bridge area on the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, there was a -- there was a special military police unit there while I operated in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what were they wearing in terms of uniform?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: There was like a new uniform, what appeared to be a very new uniform at the time, like a blue camouflage uniform. They had been issued with a new blue flak -- like a flak jacket, blue helmets, and organised into, you know, a platoon-sized organisation that we saw, at least a platoon size in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, is that blue uniform, the blue camouflage, is that the uniform of the military police in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: From what we observed, yes, that's -- that was our impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And skipping forward slightly, did you ever see those uniforms, those blue camouflage uniforms, when you were in Srebrenica, in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask for an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document which consists of two pages, one in Serbo-Croat, the other one in English, being a translation of the former, ERN 04373565 is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D896.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back again to your report. I'm not sure if you still have it in front of you, D894.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We see the following about halfway down. "When I arrived at the Zvornik bridge on the 12th April," which should be 12th of March, as you told us, "the French General Morillon had moved into the Srebrenica enclave. We tried for two weeks to get aid in as the people were starving and only the strong could get the food being dropped in by air." My question is: What are who prevented you from entering Srebrenica in those two weeks?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb forces delayed us for that two-week period to go into Srebrenica. We would try to cross and they would tell us through a liaison officer predominantly that we could go. And when the day came or the next morning there would be some excuse, or they wouldn't show up at the bridge, and they would delay us. And then by the time they would say, Okay, you can go, it would be too late or too dangerous to go because it was getting close to night-time. And this happened for that full two-week period.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And which military unit, if any, were you dealing with in terms of entering Srebrenica on the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And who specifically were you dealing with -- well, aside from the liaison officer, who was the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: The commander or the head guy that we dealt with was Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was an escort, a UN escort, for this aid convoy also waiting in Serbia to enter Srebrenica for those two weeks?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, there was a humanitarian aid convoy came to the Zvornik bridge led by a UNHCR convoy leader, and the security force or the escort force that was with the convoy was a Canadian infantry company of approximately 120 personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that company of Canadian infantry allowed into Srebrenica by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That was one of the items of contention. They said they would not allow that infantry company to escort the convoy in. They said that they could provide security and the Bosnians would really be the danger to the convoy. Eventually when we did get into Srebrenica, all they allowed -- all they would allow to move down to Srebrenica was one APC, one armoured personnel carrier, with six or seven Canadian soldiers, military observers, and the convoy itself of civilian trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a new exhibit, with the assistance of the usher. In fact, we'll have four new exhibits on this theme, and this first one, just for the record, is 00077918 to 00077924.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And once you have that in front of you, I'm going to read a number of portions from this document. Now, first as a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, this same comment I made earlier on in regard to this document. If you intended to have it tendered and filed in -- under seal, then we won't put it on the ELMO. If not, we will put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. No, I don't propose to apply to have this kept under seal. There are a number of similar documents which we have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it can be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, first, as a former member of a mission in Bosnia, can you please explain how the dates and times are set out in this and similar documents. We see in the top right-hand corner where it says date 07 1625, A MAR 93. What date and time does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That would be known as what we call in the military a date/time group because there's many documents go out on any 24-hour period, you actually add the time that you finish this document. So you would have the date, 07, which would be the seventh day, at 1625 hours. The A would be the time -- the local time, and March. And then the year, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. So in other words, you in fact have the time sort of sandwiched in between the date and the month in these documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this then is dated 7th of March, 1993, and the period covered is the previous seven days, the 1st of the 7th of March, 1993, as we see the period covered. I'm going to read firstly just the general situation. "The Command Area of Responsibility (AOR) was relatively stable with the exceptions of Sarajevo and the East Bosnian enclaves. Whether the past 7 day lull of combat activity in Sarajevo is due to the weather or the latest ceasefire attempts is too early to say. International focus has, in any event, shifted to the East Bosnian Muslim enclaves where the Serb offensive into the Cerska and Srebrenica areas appears to have accelerated its timetable, coincident with US aid airdrops." And then if we turn to page 5 of 9C, Eastern Bosnia, this is the assessment, we see, "The enclaves of Cerska, Srebrenica and possibly Zepa are clearly being ethnically cleansed by BSA forces, with JNA support. US airdrop program appears to have accelerated the BSA timetable by several weeks. In any event, Serb forces will likely resist entry of UNPROFOR and UNHCR elements into the more sensitive parts of the enclaves." Now, I'd simply ask, was that -- what's written there, was that what was reflected in your experience of trying to get into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was that, as this report suggests, because the Srebrenica enclave was being ethnically cleansed by the Serbs and the Serbs didn't want there to be any witnesses?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I didn't actually see that at that period. But on the 12th of March the outer line, if you would, of the Srebrenica pocket to the north was Konjevic Polje. When I went into Srebrenica on the 27th of March, the line was now down near Potocari. So it had obviously been cleared that distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. This document which consists of seven pages with ERN 00077918 to 924, both pages included, in the English language, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D897.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And we have the next exhibit which is 04362998, the ERN. And this is a Bratunac Brigade command dated 25 November 1992 to the Drina Corps command. It's a report for 25 November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we see at point 5: "UNPROFOR is in Ljubovija. They expect to cross tomorrow." At 7, "The Turks are entering minefields and getting killed." And 8: "I would like to ask you to do your best to prevent UNPROFOR from passing through. As an officer and acting on behalf of the people, I will not let them pass through, even at the cost of being replaced. I hope you will understand me. Lieutenant Colonel Borivoje Tesic." Now, this obviously refers to November 1992, a little while before you got there, but it reflects, does it not, obstruction on the part of the Serbs to the movement of UNPROFOR in November 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it would reflect the continued delay -- delaying efforts for us to go into Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Actually, in the interests of time I'll ask for an exhibit number for this document and move to the next exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document which consists of two pages, one in Serbo-Croat, the ERN 04362998, and the other being the English translation thereof, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D898.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The next exhibit is 04363002. And again, for the record, this is Bratunac Brigade command. Date, 27 November 1992, Drina Corps command. And we see at 5: "We have heard that UNPROFOR intends to pass through Skelani. Do not do this. The people here will rise up. Do not feed the Muslims. Later we fight with them, regardless of the depth of political aims."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, first if we look at the map, I don't know if you know where Skelani is, but if possible I would like you to mark that on D895. I don't know if you can locate Bajina Basta first of all. And I'm sure there will be no direction if I direct you if you have any difficulties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Jones, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you go to Ljubovija and follow the Drina down south, you'll see Bajina Basta.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's on the Serbian side. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If you could just mark Skelani, on the other side please.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we saw the words in this document "do not feed the Muslims." Did you understand that to be part of the Serbs' aim in blocking UNPROFOR from entering Srebrenica when you were there in March 1993? In other words, that they were essentially trying to starve the Muslims into submission?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, the fact that they would not allow the humanitarian aid convoys to get in or to get in on a regular basis and the fact that the US air force had to drop food, then that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, which like the previous one consists of two pages, one in B/C/S, the other one in English, being the translation thereof, with ERN 04363002 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D899.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the next exhibit is being distributed which is 04261938 to 04261939.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you'll see reference here to Skelani and Bajina Basta municipality, so you'll see why I was asking you to mark those on the map. This is from the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff. It's dated 2nd February 1993. Submit to Drina Corps command. And then: "Based on the report, the 35th POB command dated 27 January 1993, a report of the commission that compiled an infantry list of weapons and ammunition in the storage of Bajina Basta municipality, which belongs to Skelani municipality, you are to act as follows: For the needs of Drina Corps take the following types and quantities of weapons and types of ammunition from the above-mentioned storage." And this is signed by the assistant logistics commander Major General Djordje Djukic, and there's a list of weapons and ammunition. Well, firstly, while I don't think it's in dispute that Bajina Basta is in Skelani and Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to this, weapons of the Bosnian Serb army were stored in Serbia. Is that correct first of all?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: It appears to say that on this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we see a reference to a slow-burning fuse, and you'll see that at number 33 right towards the end. Is that the same thing as a delayed fuse?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No. A slow-burning fuse is a fuse used to actually set off a charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I'll ask simply for an exhibit number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. This document which consists of two pages in Serbo-Croat with ERN 04261938 to 939 and three pages in English is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D900.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I think finally before the break we can deal with the last of these exhibits it's 04292356 to 04292357. And this is again command of the Drina Corps, dated 25 November 1992. And subject is: "Passage of UNPROFOR through the corps' zone," and it's to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, personally to the commander. And I read: "General" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly are you aware who this would be addressed to if we're talking about the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Not exactly, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Have you heard of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it could refer to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It says: "General, over and above all the tasks that we have been accomplishing to the best of our best of our abilities, according to plan, additional obligations have been imposed on us, probably according to somebody's plan according to UNPROFOR's forces. These are, for instance," and I'm skipping down a couple of paragraphs and past those examples. It says: "The Serbian people throughout the Podrinje region categorically refuse to accept aid from executioners. "I would like to ask you to listen to the appeal from the people of the Podrinje, who trust you to a man, not to allow UNPROFOR to enter Srebrenica under any circumstances because if various journalists do enter Srebrenica, they will raise the issue of this town to the level of Sarajevo issue. "It is not true that the Muslims of Srebrenica are starving because the Serbian villages were too rich to bring the Turks of those villages to starvation so soon." Now, dealing with that phrase, that sentence "do not allow UNPROFOR to enter Srebrenica because the issue of the town will be raised to Sarajevo," you spent time in Sarajevo as an UNMO. When you were there was the siege and shelling and sniping world news?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, the siege of Sarajevo was world news, probably on a daily basis for a long time and Srebrenica probably did not get a lot of the world press, due to the events that were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: When you were in Srebrenica in March and April 1993, did the situation become a matter of international concern?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it did because of General Morillon being the commander of the UN forces in Bosnia getting into Srebrenica, that became something of interest to the world press. So on a daily basis, we would listen to BBC radio and there was lots of information coming across the radio as well as the television and I'm sure the newspapers on what was going on down in Srebrenica, especially due to the fact that Srebrenica was now getting smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So does it seem plausible to you that the Serbs didn't want the world to know what was going on in Srebrenica, for fear that there would be an outcry?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, as long as there was no UN forces observing, then any force could do whatever they wanted and more or less get away with it. But when military observers who were in any location, then that was our job to observe and report, and our daily reports went back to the United Nations' headquarters in New York.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we also saw the words there "the Serbian people throughout the Podrinje region categorically refused to accept aid from executioners." Now, did you come across Serb hostility to UNPROFOR when you were in Eastern Bosnia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, pretty much on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you mention just a couple examples, perhaps, of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: On the 12th of March when I arrived at Zvornik bridge, I mentioned earlier that I had gone immediately to the hotel. And after we had lunch that day, we got a call on the radio to go down the Serb side of the Drina, try to get to Ljubovija to make radio contact with the military observers, and General Morillon in -- that had actually got into Srebrenica, or at least that was what we thought at that time. However, about halfway from Zvornik bridge to Ljubovija we were stopped by a JNA soldier. He was about to shoot us, and there was an old -- older man that was essentially edging him on and he was yelling in his language to shoot us. This soldier eventually cut off the radio handset from our vehicle so we couldn't make communications, and he took one of the military observer's ID cards. And at that point we decided it was probably better to go back, as you can imagine. Also, on two occasions on the Bosnian Serb side, my vehicle had been surrounded by thousands of women. And we thought they were going to flip the vehicle and lynch us, essentially. On one occasion my interpreter was able to say something to them so we could get away, and this is a very scary type of incident when you have a crowd and they just basically edge themselves on and you don't know what will happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you ever encounter any sort of hostility of that nature on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, but not on the -- not at that type of level. Sometimes on an individual basis, but certainly not at that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally, just to clarify one matter. You said the soldier eventually cut off the radio handset. Are you talking about the physical act of cutting it off? And if so, what did he use to do that?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. As a military observer we had two types of radios. We would have a hand-held radio which was just -- you would just recharge the battery. And we also had a vehicle-mounted radio that takes it power off the vehicle battery, and it has a microphone that's attached to the radio with a long cord. The driver had taken the handset to talk, and this soldier reached in, grabbed the handset, and then with his AK-47 bayonet cut the wire and at that point we lost communications because that was all we had at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. I would simply ask for an exhibit number and we can take a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this document which consists of two pages in B/C/S, two pages in English, ERN 04292356 to 357 is, being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D901. We will have a break, Captain, now for 30 minutes. We will resume soon after. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, Captain MacDonald, I'm going to move now to your stay in Srebrenica. You told us this morning that you stayed from the 27th of March, 1993, approximately, until the 4th of April, 1993. Do you -- who did you go into -- sorry. With whom did you go into Srebrenica? Did you go on your own or did you go in a group of people?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I went in with a team or what we call two teams of military observers. I don't know if you want their names or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No. No, thank you. And do they travel in one or two vehicles? How does that work?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: We were in, I recall, two vehicles. We travelled in Toyota Land Cruisers, and there would have been three military observers per vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was there already a UN presence in Srebrenica when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Some of the -- some of the personnel who had gotten in with General Morillon stayed in. So there was actually, I believe, one Canadian soldier that stayed in and there was some -- I think there was somebody from UNHCR. So there was a limited UN presence that stayed in from General Morillon's initial entry to the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where were they headquartered in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: We were headquartered in the PTT building in the centre part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And was anything done by the UN to mark off the PTT building as the UN's headquarters in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: There was two ways that we designated or was designated that that building was a UN headquarters. We had raised the UN flag on the roof of the PTT building, as well, initially, there was a lot of people trying to look in the windows and come to the door to get in to ask for food or whatever, so the Canadian soldiers put up a boundary away from the building which designated -- you weren't allowed to cross that line, again, for our security. So there was a rope and some sticks put up to designate that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And during the seven or so days that you were in Srebrenica, what was your main task, you personally, and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I was tasked as the communications officer, as well to monitor the situation with our vehicles for refueling, any maintenance that we could do. That was of course on a limited basis. But predominantly I was responsible for communications and patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So you were doing lots of radio checks and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, on a daily basis there was a location up on the -- it would have been the south-west side, I guess, of the town itself. That was a high feature, and we would go up there and we could get some kind of communications with any military observers that would have been moving down from Zvornik area, and particularly if there was a convoy coming and they would have military observer escort, then we would be able to talk to them at a certain point once they got in range of the radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to come back to radio communications in a second. But firstly, just to clarify this, was your mission, and again you personally, concerned in any way of finding out who had power, civilian or military power or authority, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Not specifically. As I was not the team leader of the group, I was not specifically designated with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right that during your time in Srebrenica you didn't form any particular impression of who, if anyone, had power or authority in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to the question of radio communications. You mentioned radios this morning. You might have mentioned hand-held radios. Did you have hand-held radios? And if so, what type?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: We had a limited number of hand-held radios. They are or they were Motorola radios, if you know the brand, and a hand-held Motorola radio has a limited range of approximately two to three kilometres. And the range is limited to line of sight, which means you have to be able to essentially see the other person. If there's a mountain in the way, that's not line of sight. The signal cannot go over the mountain. But anything that might be in the way may limit the range of that radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've told us earlier how -- that the area is a mountainous terrain. Would it be right that it was not easy to establish communications with those Motorolas?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: It was extremely difficult to establish radio communications, and also as I mentioned there was no repeaters, no UN repeater, in that location. So we were limited to the range of the radio itself. Due to the terrain, that made communications even weaker than normal. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And if you know, roughly how much does it cost to construct a repeater?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: One repeater tower, just the tower alone, might be up to 100.000 dollars, US dollars. So if you add the actual repeater on to the tower, we're talking way over 100.000 dollars US, just for one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is it right that part of what the UN was doing in Bosnia at the beginning of the conflict was to construct repeaters?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. That would have been one of the first things that the UN did earlier in 1992, it would have been to set up repeaters in as many locations as possible throughout former Yugoslavia so that we could expand our radio communications. With a repeater, it enhances your signal for even the hand-held radio, making the range even greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And those were being constructed, I take it, either because they didn't exist or because either repeaters had been damaged or destroyed. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: If somebody doesn't want you to put a repeater in their area of responsibility, then they might give you difficulties. I don't know why exactly there was no repeaters in that area, but, you know, you can speculate from there. Also, just to clarify, if you don't exactly understand what a repeater is, imagine the cellphone. Everybody has cellphones these days. It does a very similar concept to a cellphone satellite or the signal is exchanged and then passed on to another location. So it expands the location that you can talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: But, as you've told us, those didn't exist in the Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Not in that area, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back to your report again for a brief moment. You still have it with you, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And it's right towards the bottom there's an extract which reads: "When our team arrived the movement was severely restricted because of the waist-deep snow which had just fallen. The Serbs were attacking on all sides and slowly squeezing the pocket smaller and smaller, looting and then burning the Muslim homes as they went. As military observers, we could only watch and report." Now, firstly, is that an accurate summary of the situation as you found it when you arrived in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And I personally observed this to be happening while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we see it written there "the Serbs were attacking on all sides and slowly squeezing the pocket smaller and smaller." Would you describe Srebrenica as being under siege at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in that regard I would like you to look at a new exhibit with the usher's assistance with the ERN 00077911 to 00077917. And this is dated 15th March, 1993. And again, as before I'm not applying for this to be under seal so it can be placed on ELMO. And it covers the period from, I believe, the 7th to the 15th of March. And it says: "The general situation. The area of operations was quiet other than in Sarajevo and the eastern enclaves where the media continues to focus international attention." Then I'll go to page 2 and it's points 3A and B and then the first sentence of C. Eastern Bosnia. "The systematic cleansing of the Srebrenica enclave continues in the form of a strong BSA offensive. It appears that the Serbs are advancing from the north and east simultaneously. With the fall of Cerska this week, BSA forces pushed east and south, pressuring Konjevic Polje and Srebrenica respectively. "B, the situation in Srebrenica is reported as being desperate as civilian refugees are concentrating there. There are a large number of wounded, and they are reportedly without medicine and anaesthetics. "C, the condition of the Srebrenica defence is not clear amid media reports of its imminent collapse." Now, does this describe the military and civilian situation as you arrived on the 27th of March, 1993, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In short, there was a strong Bosnian Serb Army offensive?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Correct, particularly on the 3rd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And the Serbs were advancing from several directions?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And this was creating an even further influx of refugees into the pocket?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Anybody who had not actually come into Srebrenica by that point would have been probably on the move that particular day to finally come in because most of the area was taken on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. This document which consists of seven pages and is in English with ERN 00077911 to 917 is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D902.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have two more exhibits in this sequence. The next one has an ERN 00077904 to 00077910. And this is dated the 22nd of March, 1993, 1400 hours.
