And again, the period covered is from the 14th to the 20th of March, 1993. General situation: "The situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina is critically tense. Fighting throughout the AOR continues at its normally intense levels. Although conditions in the Srebrenica enclave have improved as the commander as won concessions from the Serbs and Serbians to get aid into the enclave, wounded persons, women and children extracted, the Serbs continue to squeeze the refugees into an every-tightening noose. Fierce fighting throughout Sarajevo is unabated." Then turning to page 2. I'll direct your attention to 3A: "The systematic cleansing of the Srebrenica enclave continued this week with the same strong BSA offensive launched ten days ago. This offensive has been made by closing in on Srebrenica on the main routes. They have received a lot of support from across the boarder in Serbia throughout this offensive. It seems likely that some of the forces involved in this operation, particularly those attacking from across the river, were FRY soldiers. The Serbians have also supported the BSA with heavy artillery, some unsophisticated aircraft bombers, and ammunition resupply convoys." Now, this document refers to the Bosnian Serb army receiving support from Serbia proper. First, in the form of heavy artillery, and that's something you've told us you saw with your own eyes in mid-March 1993. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Then second, support from unsophisticated aircraft bombers. Now, is that something which you saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. We had heard that there was coming taking place and were unable to confirm it. And then one day when I had actually been able to get through the checkpoint on the way to Ljubovija on the Serb side, I saw a small biplane carrying cluster bombs flying from inside Serbia across the Drina to Srebrenica. So that was confirmation from where the aircraft were coming from, and when I got into Srebrenica I had actually seen the cluster bomb casings which kind of tied it all up, that they were in fact bombing from inside Serbia. These aircraft would have been flying below NATO radar at tree-top level. So it would have been very hard for a NATO AWAC's aircraft to pick these up.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And third, this document refers to support in the form of ammunition resupply convoys, support from Serbia. Is that something to which you can attest?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. On that one occasion that I had mentioned earlier about sitting in my vehicle in Ljubovija and watching trucks for well over an hour move to the east towards Bosnia, the tarps in the back of the truck were not tied and I saw ammunition crates, fresh ammunition crates in the back, which I believed to be 120-millimetre and 122-millimetre mortars. And also I saw troops moving across the dam just to the south of Zvornik on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, on page 1 of this document we saw it stated: "The Serbs continued to squeeze the refugees into an ever-tightening noose." You said Srebrenica was under siege at this time. Was this description of an ever-tightening noose accurate when you were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it would be extremely accurate. And although they continued to not let us in as I mentioned earlier, the line of conflict had been initially around Konjevic Polje on the 12th. And again, when I went in on the 27th, it was now at Potocari, in that area. So we deduced that it had to have been systematic in taking that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I want to explore this, the notion of a siege with you in some more detail. First, are you familiar in military terminology with the expression "depth," and, if so, if you can explain what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, depth is something we always try to achieve, whether we're conducting offensive operations or, more importantly, defensive operations. To describe depth, it means deep, and instead of just having one line that, if somebody breaks through, I have successive lines and, I would say, in depth. So if somebody breaks through one area, then I have another force immediately behind that can hopefully stop them. And the more depth that I have, the better. However, with limited forces, my depth sometimes may not be as good as I would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when it comes to a siege, would depth then refer to having several lines around a besieged area?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, of course any commander would want to try and do that if they had the personnel to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And on that theme I want to go back to an earlier part of your testimony when you referred to seeing these bunkers on the road from Pale to Zvornik. And you told us that that was to prevent refugees from Srebrenica getting through to Tuzla. An obvious question, but was that, in your opinion, linked to the siege of Srebrenica or not, those bunkers?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to the 12th of March, the Sebesic pocket confrontation line would have been in the northern area close to that road. So therefore, the -- that line would have been a Bosnian Serb defensive line.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Defensive but enforcing a siege. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would just ask for an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, Mr. Jones, which consists of seven pages with ERN 00077904 to 910, all seven pages are in the English language, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D903.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And now, lastly in this sequence of exhibits we have ERN 00077889 to 00077895. This is dated 29th March, 1993, so dealing with the period when you were actually in Srebrenica, and it's covering the period from the 22nd of March to the 28th of March. I'll just read the general situation. "Intense combat activity throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina marked the beginning of the reporting period, particularly in northern and Eastern Bosnia and in Sarajevo." And in fact, the rest of that paragraph isn't relevant for our purposes. And then page 2, 3, Eastern Bosnia, I'll just read the first two sentences. "The BSA offensive into the Srebrenica enclave continued its apparently inexorable drive towards the centre at Srebrenica from the north, south, and south-east. Muslim towns and villages continue to fall in an almost systematic fashion as BiH local commanders attempted to hold the line." Now, can you comment on that reference to a systematic fashion which Muslim towns and villages were falling to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Basically what we deduced from what happened in Konjevic Polje on the 12th and the fact that that area between Konjevic Polje and Potocari, and, obviously, anywhere else in that circle, plus what I had been told by a Bosnian Serb commander who I'd mentioned earlier, Vinko Pandurevic, they would have to clear each village. Because if there was Bosnian forces in a village, in military terms you have to clear the village. Urban fighting is very fierce, and once a village would have been taken and cleared and then held, then they would move on. And on the 3rd of April, I actually saw this taking place in the south -- southern area of Srebrenica. So some of this was deduced based on reports and what we knew, and then eyewitness report from myself on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And then how did use of artillery fit in with this pattern of taking villages?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, the Bosnian Serb forces didn't have a lot of infantry, but they had a lot of -- or a lot more of artillery and tanks and equipment, whereas the Bosnian forces had tens of thousands of men that could fight, however they didn't have a lot of artillery and tanks. Even small arms they didn't have a lot of. The Serb forces, the Bosnian Serb forces didn't necessarily want to take casualties. So it was easier for them and they had had a -- lots of support, of course ammunition. What they would do is bomb a village -- and again, we seen this in Konjevic Polje, bomb a village until everybody essentially left. And then it was easy for their limited amount of infantry forces to come in and clear that village. And I think they actually hoped that there would be nobody left, but anybody that was left would have been executed. And this was part of the systematic way to clean a village. The villages would have been then looted and destroyed, or at least partly destroyed. They may have set fires to the village with their attack or possibly afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So is it right then from what you've said that because the Bosnian Serb forces didn't want -- particularly didn't want to take any casualties because they had a manpower shortage, that they favoured the use of artillery on a large scale in order to avoid those casualties?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that's what we deduced based on our investigations, patrolling, and information that we got during my time in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you said that on the Bosnian side there were tens of thousands of men that could fight. Are you speaking about men who actually in properly formed military units, or men of military age who could be involved in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Civilians --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The objection is the quoting of the witness. The Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness didn't use the word "the Bosnian side," but rather referred to. And may I take a look at the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bosnian Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Bosnian forces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you look at page -- the previous page, line 5 or 6, you will see that he is referring to the Serb forces, the Bosnian Serb forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: The Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which page? All right. I have to look at it. Yeah, yeah, but that's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think colloquially we refer to the Bosnian Side and the Bosnian Serb side. I don't see the force of the objection. I think the practice is that my learned friend is meant to wait for an indication before interrupting the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it was about the correct quotation of the witness and that's what I would like to refer my learned friend to. And I thought the right quotation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what's the objection at the end of it? What difference does it make?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Just Bosnians or when the witness used the qualification "Bosnian army" or "Bosnian forces," that makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He didn't say Bosnian army. Now my learned friend is misquoting. He's doing precisely what he's accused me of doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can follow --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can put the question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do. Let's finish with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is an objection from my learned friend, and it's disingenuous to pretend that it's an interpretation issue. That's the exception which Your Honour made, where an objection can be stated straight away, id it's a problem with interpretation. I'm speaking English, the witness is speaking English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But I could sense what he was referring to, what he was objecting to is something that is contained in the question itself. That's why --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As all objections are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not always. Many a time they aren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just would insist on a similar treatment on both sides, that we have a clear rule that my learned friend doesn't just stand up and object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but you understand, Mr. Jones, that the Trial Chamber has to reserve for itself a lot of discretion here and there is a lot of difference, as I am sure you are aware of, coming from a common-law jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In any event, Captain MacDonald, I think you understood my question because you started to answer it. What would your answer be.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: You lost me. You're going to have to ask me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply this: When you were referring to -- and I'll quote. You said that there were tens of thousands -- in fact, I'm going to have to find the quote now. You said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: "Whereas the Bosnian forces had tens of thousands of men that could fight." Could you elaborate precisely what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, I had seen it in Sarajevo and then again in Srebrenica. Any man that was fit and -- it wouldn't be of -- necessarily of military age. I've seen young boys up to older men that basically were defending their towns and their families. And they would be maybe armed with a rifle. So there was lots of people that wanted to defend themselves. So that -- hence the tens of thousands, I mean there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So basically there were more Muslims than Serbs, and that's what you were referring to in terms of numerical superiority?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: When it came to somebody fighting and able to hold terrain. So a man actually standing in a trench or standing on a line, defending.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you've referred to the fact that the Serbs were not -- not prepared, I mean as any army, but particularly not prepared to take casualties. Did that have an effect on their way of fighting, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, again, if you fire enough artillery at somebody, they're going to leave. They're either going to get killed, they're going to have to get down inside a trench or a bunker, or flee. And if you're not military, you're going to flee, if you shoot enough artillery rounds into a village. Plus, artillery rounds are going to destroy, you know, electricity wires, water, anything that you might have. And if they do set fire to the village, then you're going to leave as well. So it was easier for them, we believed, to just fire the artillery and then, as we call, mop-up in the end with your infantry forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, going back to this document it continues in section 3A: "The following built-up areas were reported fallen to the Serbs this week, Ljeskovic, Karacici, and Gajici. The villages Osmace and Subin were last reported surrounded by BSA forces. Fighting was reported in and around Zeleni Jadar, the Serbs in the town itself on 25 March." Now, are you familiar with some of the places, for example, Osmace and Zeleni Jadar?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Zeleni Jadar in particular because that's where I had gone on foot patrol. On the 28th of March I had gone on a foot patrol down to Zeleni Jadar. There was too much snow to drive. And then on the 3rd of April I went to Zeleni Jadar where I was wounded. There was a big attack going on there. And I had heard of Osmace while I was in Srebrenica. The other villages I don't specifically remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. And we have a new map which shows the Srebrenica area, in particular, with any luck, Zeleni Jadar. So I will ask if you can find, when that's passed up, those locations and just mark it with a highlighter. So if you could firstly locate Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: On the map it just says Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You described how when you were there you saw a village burning. All right. Could you indicate that village on the map, please, and the name of the village, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Turanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I believe it says Turanj on the map, but no doubt it's the same location. And Osmace, are you familiar with Osmace and able to locate that on the map.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So was it in this area then that you noticed this particularly strong offensive on the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. On the 3rd of April there was a -- there had been a cease-fire or more or less a cease-fire, in loose terms. On the 3rd of April the Bosnian Serbs were on the move again making a major offensive action. And I went down to the hill just to the north of Zeleni Jadar on that morning and observed a major attack going on, artillery in particular firing into Zeleni Jadar. Bosnian men behind the hill getting ready to, I don't know, counter-attack or maybe withdraw. And that village Turanj or Toranje was being burned. And I observed through my binoculars Bosnian Serb soldiers looting and destroying that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to come back to that instant where you were wounded in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I would ask for an exhibit number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we haven't given a number to the previous document either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I have finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the previous one. So the document which was previously made use of by the Defence which consists of seven pages, again, with ERN 00077889 to 895, the English language, is being tendered and marked as Defence Exhibit D904. While the map that has just been marked upon by the witness is being tendered and received as Defence Exhibit D905.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you've referred already in your testimony to Serb planes flying from Serbia proper, this biplane, and then you later saw evidence that cluster bombs had been dropped. Where, in fact, did you see those casings of cluster bombs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Somebody had found the casings and brought them to the PTT building in Srebrenica. And the day or the next day that I had got into Srebrenica, so probably on the 28th of March. I had some personal interests since I had been the one saw the plane flying to verify that there was in fact evidence and we would have considered these casings to be evidence. They had Cyrillic markings on them, which may have been proof that they had come from Serbia. And that would have been something for us to put into our report to tie or to link all these things together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to show you a portion of a video, and it's Defence Exhibit 111. First I'll ask you to look at it and then I'll have a couple of questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, just for the record, this is at 09.00, I believe, on this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I can't see that from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We can see it now in very small green numbering in the bottom right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So the still that is being shown to the witness from Defence Exhibit 111, D111, is at 09.00, and it shows a biplane.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we'll just play a few seconds of this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, firstly, did you see a plane in this video clip that we just saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. That exact type of plane was the one that I had seen flying across from Serbia into Bosnia on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in what we saw just now did you see that plane dropping a bomb?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: In the video?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In the video, that plane dropped a bomb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you able to tell - and we can replay the video a few times if you like - what sort of a bomb it dropped?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: There would have been different types of bombs. It could have been a cluster bomb or it could have just been a bomb that just would gone off when it landed. A cluster bomb being a bomb that has sub-munitions or many small bomblets, and it can cover more of an area. But it could also drop just a single bomb that would explode when it hit its target.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We will play it again and see if you can notice any characteristics of the bomb when it's being dropped.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you see the bomb appear to disappear practically from sight at one point?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation of what might be happening there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: There appeared to be that the casings fly off. At one point, you may have been seen on there what appeared to be two things flying off to the side, so it appears to be a cluster bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We're finished with that video and in fact moving to a different area. Are you able to tell us roughly how many people were in Srebrenica at the time when you were there in March 1993, in the whole enclave?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: When I went to Srebrenica on the 27th of March, we estimated there to be around 30.000 people in the town itself, down inside the town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And where were they sleeping? Where were they accommodated?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: People were sleeping in any of the buildings that they could get a spot to sleep, the schools, any buildings that may have been abandoned, but there was a large majority of the people sleeping in the streets anywheres where they could find a spot to lay down.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was the temperature like at this time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: One or two days prior to me going into Srebrenica there was a big snow storm or a heavy snow fall, if you would. Even down in Banja Koviljaca we got a lot of snow. Being a mountainous region. I estimated -- although the snow was waist-deep, in some places up to my waist, so in some places up to a metre deep. And the temperature dropped, particularly at night-time, so you would have had done to 0, maybe below, you know, below freezing, but extremely cold for people who didn't have anything or were sleeping outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you, yourself, actually see anyone who had succumbed to the cold?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I went on foot patrol one morning and saw two bodies where people had died that night, probably in their sleep that night, and the bodies were just laying in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was that an unusual sight, something which caused concern among the local population?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I don't think so because everybody was concerned for their own, probably, well-being at that point. And the bodies at that point hadn't been moved. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you see many children among the refugees?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: We seen a lot of children that appeared to be alone and be without parents, particularly one little boy who hung around our -- the PTT building begging for food and whatnot. And I think somebody had talked to him and he said his parents had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So there were unsupervised children, in essence, in the town of Srebrenica. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That is correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, it's not in dispute, I believe, that people were starving in Srebrenica at this time. And you've told us how the Serbs obstructed food convoys from entering the enclave. It may be an obvious question, but why do you suppose the Serbs were not allowing food into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I wouldn't really be able to say why, but, I mean, if you're trying to starve somebody, you're trying to make them submit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It was about the leading and speculative character of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not speculation. If he has an explanation as a military observer on something which is fundamental military efforts ... Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that starving, to make someone submit, is that a classic albeit, now, illegal [Realtime transcript read in error "legal"] siege tactic?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Certainly that would be a tactic in making somebody submit. If you're blocking off the roads so they can't get food, they're not letting UN convoys in, and it would probably be obvious that if the Americans had to drop rations from the sky, that was the only way to get food into the people to try and keep them alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just for the transcript I said "illegal."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That didn't really answer your question, but let's move, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You mentioned rations being dropped from the sky. In what form was that being dropped?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Initially the US air force was dropping rations, military rations, known as MREs, or meals ready to eat, on pallets and they were basically coming out of the back of a Hercules aircraft by parachute. Some of these palates were floating into the sides of mountains into Bosnian Serb territory where they couldn't be reached. So when I went in, they started changing the delivery method and were just dropping them out of the back of the planes. So they weren't on parachutes and it was more accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, was it actually safe for civilians from Srebrenica to go up and wait for MREs to be dropped from the sky?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Certainly not. If you were up in the area of the drop and you were hit by one of these ration packs or boxes or any debris that would have been coming out of the plane, then you would be undoubtedly killed. So we used to warn the people the best we could to stay away from the drop area until after the drop was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did they heed those warnings?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No. There was still people up there and we had -- we had heard that some people actually had been killed by some rations dropping out of the sky.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So in other words, you warned civilians not to go to find food on the hills because there was mortal danger involved, but they went anyway?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was control of these people, these refugees, actually possible in Srebrenica at this time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. And I didn't see any possibility while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that regard I want to ask you about another incident. Were you present when a convoy, UN convoy, came into Srebrenica and then people were evacuated from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I was involved in that convoy coming in and then the people going out on the trucks to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we're going to play a short segment of a video, it's Defence Exhibit 700, D700, if you just watch the video. Yes, I believe we need to ask for the sound to be switched on from the booth for Defence Exhibit mode.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Interviewer: "We've set the stage for it. What is it we're going to see next. Tony Birtley: "I think we're going to see one of the scenes that will stay with me and I think for the people who saw the video for many, many, many years and that is the sight of complete and you are the desperation of people who simply want to get out of a situation and are prepared to do anything to do that. "I couldn't believe what I was seeing. I think sometimes in journalism we can be warped to steer towards hyperbole, but, you know, there's nothing you could say to really describe what was going on, the sheer panic and the desperation of those people. And to see women throw their babies into the back of a truck and hoping that somebody would grab them and take them to safety, because separation for them was far better than having a youngster endure starvation and shells and bullets, was terrible, really. Scenes of people getting angry before the convoy left. The UN heard about it, but they could do nothing. I think people have become so desperate that they're prepared to do absolutely anything. I think it's on the lowest level of humanity. I think these people are prepared to steal, even kill to survive because nobody else is looking after them."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Firstly, are those scenes familiar to you? Is that the sort of thing you saw on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I was there that day. I was in that crowd.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we heard -- actually, do you recognise the journalist who is speaking there from his bed?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Tony Birtley. He was there at the time when I went there and previous when I had gone in on the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You would have heard him say that the UN heard about what was going on there but could do nothing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That would have been correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And you might have also heard him expressing the opinion that the people there were prepared to do anything simply to survive. Is that a sentiment which you share?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, we saw in that video attempts by -- or at least an attempt by a man shooting a rifle in the air to try and control the crowd. Is that something which you saw?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, on the particular morning when the people got in the back of the trucks, I was standing beside one of those guys and some people had actually gotten on the trucks that night. The convoy had come in the day before. They offloaded the supplies, and then it was too dangerous for the civilian drivers to go back across the confrontation line. So there was a few men designated to try and guard the trucks, but a few men weren't able to do that. And then a number of times you saw on the video where he fired in the air to try and get the crowd to go back. But as soon as they fired in the air and then it stopped, the crowd would surge back onto the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Is there any reason you were standing near the man shooting into the air?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, because that would be the safest place to be. Because when the bullets are fired in the air they are going to come back down and possibly kill people in the vicinity. However, due to the velocity and the -- particularly the wind speed the bullet would not come down on that person who fired it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So again, as with the air drop situation, was there a deadly risk to people remaining in the area, but they remained nonetheless?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, and due to the size of the crowd there was a very good chance that people were killed in the crowd, and that's what we had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Again, was there any possibility of controlling this crowd of people?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: None whatsoever, no. Not without a larger force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And even with a larger force, what, in fact, could be done to prevent people climbing on these trucks?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: You would have essentially had to have such a large force that they would have been able to go shoulder to shoulder. And even then, if you have a crowd of 20 or 30.000 people pushing, then you can't stop it, just the pure weight of the crowd. So you would almost have to shoot people to stop, and they were not -- I don't think prepared to do that to their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right. Now, moving to a slightly different area. We're finished with that video. You mentioned earlier in your testimony people involved in the defence of their homes and their families in Srebrenica, Muslims. Did you see uniforms, military uniforms, when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Not really. Some people had uniforms that they may have procured through some means. Most people were in civilian clothing, and some men may have had bits and pieces of a uniform. But there was no formed -- no set uniform as such that a military force would normally have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as a military man, can you perhaps explain for us a little about the significance of a uniform and what it's important to.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, a uniform, I guess by definition, means everybody's the same, so in uniform. One of the -- one of the first things that I learned in training or that we teach people is discipline. And one of the first ways of teaching discipline is to put everybody in the same uniform, short haircuts, and try and kind of take away your individualism. It also creates pride and what's known as esprit de corps, so that's important in any formed unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So it's important to discipline, to esprit de corps. Is it important to the command structure?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. The command structure in the military is such that the leaders, of course, have different rank and going up and down what we have -- what we call a chain of command. And everybody's rank is readily visible so you know who is higher, therefore would be in charge or who was in command, given circumstances where the known leader was killed or not available.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in the Canadian forces, is it possible to just wear parts of a uniform, just, say, shirt or trousers?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No, that would be strongly forbidden. We have to wear the correct uniform all the time, and we wouldn't be allowed to mix uniform, for example. So I have to wear either my uniform, or if I'm in civilian clothing, I would only be wearing civilian clothing and not mixing the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So, at least in the Canadian forces - and I take it this applies to other NATO forces - there are very strict rules about uniform and uniform itself is critical, critical to discipline, esprit de corps, and the command structure?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, strict rules about the uniform, and that would be correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: On this subject, in a NATO member state, what would a brigade consist of?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: A brigade would consist of, like personnel-wise, 4 to 5.000 soldiers plus their equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how would they be organised in terms of battalions and in terms of having support?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Everything in a NATO structure is based on threes. So in a brigade you would have three battalions. Each of those battalions would have three companies. Each company would have three platoons. Each platoon would have three sections. So it's all based on threes. Plus a brigade would have the support for the main -- those main three elements to carry out the operations that they are tasked to do, and the four main areas of course are: Ammunition, fuel, water, food, and maintenance would be the fifth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in terms of support units, is it correct that - and I assume I'm allowed to lead on this - you would have logistics, engineers, artillery, air defence, medical support, and headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. All that stuff would be considered part of the support to the main three functional areas, or those main three. So engineers would be sub-tasked out, artillery or defence, all the logistics would be sub-tasked out to support those smaller operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be correct that whether or not a group of fighting men can be called a brigade is not just a question of manpower but of capabilities, support, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be very important, the capabilities, other than just the men alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you explain to us the concept of a "formed unit," if you're familiar with that term.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: A formed unit would be essentially, in Canadian context, a unit that has a -- what we call a TO & E, it would be a NATO term. This stands for table of equipment and organisation. So you actually have a list of the personnel that are in that unit by rank and the qualification required for that specific position. Also the list of equipment is extremely important. Also a key thing would be a command structure and a chain of command. So there would be a commanding officer at the very top level, and if you got down to those sections that I was talking about in the platoons, a section commander. So up and down there's a chain of command, and if something happens to one person, the next person in the chain of command takes over. So somebody always knows what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So this table -- these tables of organisation and equipment are also essential for a command structure. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Without an TO & E, in our context, you can't have a unit that has a proper task and knows what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now we're going to play another part of a video we saw earlier, D700, just a small segment. It's from there, and just for the record I think it's 0132 where it starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "To be a Bosnian soldier you got have -- to be resigned to defeat -- you've got to be resigned to jury, and also you've got to be resigned to death. It's a total misnomer. It is a big fight, the equivalent of Mike Tyson fighting some 15 year old with both arms tied behind his back. They simply do not have the weapons to compete on a level footing with what the Serbs have got. They have 1948, 1950s rifles, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. they have Kalashnikovs if they're lucky. They've got a couple of tanks that they captured from the Serbs but they can't fire them because they ran out of ammunition a long, long time ago."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing on that video a line of fighters marching along, walking along?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record the video was stopped at 0211.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And does that chime with what you saw at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, the fact that some people were wearing a camouflage shirt and some were just in complete civilian dress, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In your opinion were there the fighters you saw in Srebrenica in any sense a proper army, in any sense of the word?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I would say not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, can my learned friend please be more specific. "A proper army" doesn't make -- really make sense when questions are focussed on various qualifications and comparing it to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will not put the question myself, but perhaps you can put another question if you wish. I'm satisfied with the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why I said "in any sense of the word," to cover any sense of the meaning, precisely for that meaning so it would be all-encompassing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can -- just to make it obvious now, whether from what he saw he had any glimpse at all of an organised army. I mean, this is basically it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your heard his honour's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Organised armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: -- question? Would you be able to answer that?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: From what I saw there didn't appear to be a lot of organisation, even, for example, on the 3rd of April. I mean, there was just a bunch of men standing around. And I don't know who's in charge, there was no appearance of any organisation, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you to both of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, you heard Tony Birtley express the opinion there regarding the balance between the Serbs and the Muslims. "It's a total mismatch. If it were a big fight, it's the equivalent of Mike Tyson fighting some 15 year old with both arms tied behind his back." Is that something you can comment on. Do you share that opinion or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I share that opinion. Probably the best way to describe that. If you can imagine taking all the artillery and tanks away from the Bosnian Serbs and the JNA and just having, you know, men on the ground with rifles and if there was unlimited ammunition supply for both sides, the Bosnian side probably would have been able to win, even with no training and lack of, you know, properly organised units. But because of the large amounts of artillery and tanks, and of course those planes dropping bombs, that's where that example that he mentioned would -- that's the way I would describe it. You just cannot defend yourself if you don't have heavy weapons. So they did the best they could with rifles and then they would have to fall back at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, before I'm going to move on to a moment to your injury and evacuation from Srebrenica, I just want to ask you this: Did you ever meet Naser Oric when you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: One time somebody was in a meeting, one of the military observers, I believe it was our team leader and I was in the vicinity. But I didn't actually meet him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in your report that describes in detail your evacuation from Srebrenica, so I don't need to dwell on it. And in fact you've even located on the map where you were and what you saw. I think you told us that you were - and correct me if I'm wrong - that you were informed that the Zeleni Jadar area was important to the defence of Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that somebody had told us there was a water-pumping station in Zeleni Jadar. It was also a key intersection along a major route from the south. And once Zeleni Jadar fell, then there was really nothing in between there and the town of Srebrenica itself, that -- Zeleni Jadar had also been taken by the Bosnian Serbs at one point and then the Bosnian forces had actually taken it back after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And in fact, on D904 - and you don't necessarily have to have that in front of you - I'm just going to read one sentence from there, and it's the second page, 3B, last two sentences. "With the strength of the Serb drive concentrating from the south and south-east as the week progressed the Muslim southern defence line appears at this juncture to hinge on Zeleni Jadar." Is that consistent with what you were told and observed?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, your reports deals with how you were wound. If you could just tell us, firstly, how you were wounded. What weapon or what missile actually wounded you?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I was hit by shrapnel from a 120-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And as far as you're aware -- well, firstly, was that from the Serbs or from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: It was a Serb mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could you see the Serbs who were actually firing the mortars?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, we saw the mortar tube.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And could they see you?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I -- yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Did you have your blue helmets on at this time?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, we were wearing our blue helmets as well as blue -- like a blue jacket or a bib.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So were the Serbs deliberately shelling United Nations' monitors on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, wait, wait. Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben, what's your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's about this speculation on the deliberately shelling. An outcome is something else than something that you decide between your ears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to overturn your objection because the previous question was precisely tended to elicit from the witness whether they were recognisable as UN personnel, whether they were wearing the blue helmet. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can elaborate on that. I'm not sure why Mr. Wubben is concerned to defend the reputation of the Serbs from shelling monitors, but I'll pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is inappropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ignore this, please. Mr. Wubben, please ignore it. I'm ignoring it and you should ignore it, too. It's not a question of colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, if you could describe why the Serbs were deliberately shelling UN monitors?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, they were doing -- they were conducting a major attack. We were, I mean, obviously in the wrong place at the wrong time. But we could see them, I could see them, and particularly through my binoculars, so they would be able to see us. No, I could not say they deliberately targeted us, but we were targeted that day and I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact, I think, if I could refer you to your report, and it's on the second page. Do give me a moment. You refer to adjusting rounds. "Then the first of three adjusting rounds came in close." So what does that refer to, adjusting rounds?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: When you have a target, artillery is not actually 100 per cent accurate the first time you fire. So we use what we call adjusting rounds. So somebody whose map-reading skills may not be so good or they can just kind of guess where you are roughly will pick a grid and they'll fire on that grid with one round only. Once they see where that round lands, if it hasn't hit the target, they will then adjust aim from there. So when we got up at this position, one round came in, probably it was over 50 metres from where I was. The second one came in maybe 25 metres from where I was, hit me with a concussion, and then the next one came in what we call a far drop. And they're just trying to bracket in on the target slowly with the bearing and elevation of the weapons system. And once they have one that they think is close enough, they'll drop more on you and kill you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Was anyone else wounded with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Tony Birtley, the journalist, was also hit from the same mortar I was hit from. And on the second mortar there was a Bosnian man who had guided Tony Birtley and another journalist up to that position, and he was hit in the knee as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And were you taken in to the hospital, at least at some stage if not immediately?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: At some point, yes, I was evacuated down to the hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And had you seen the hospital before you went there on that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. I had gone into the hospital one time to do an assessment or on foot patrol just to see what the situation was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was the situation like there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Very dire situation in the hospital. Didn't have a lot of supplies, no electricity really, and the big thing that I recall was the smell from all the operations and blood and stuff like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Were you aware that amputations were being carried out without anaesthetics in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And how were you aware of amputations?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Canadian soldiers that came in with us on the 27th of March had been out back of the hospital building, and they came back and reported to us that there had been a pile of amputated limbs just laying there that were thrown out the window. And there was dogs and things like that, you know, trying to eat the rotten flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, who operated on you and Tony Birtley at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: The -- there was a Bosnian surgeon, there was a doctor in there at the time. I forget exactly how to pronounce his name, but he operated on me the day I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If the witness can be shown -- I'm not sure, it may be D199, it's about War Hospital, just briefly. Yes, D199. So it's not on the exhibit list, but there's a photograph which I would like him to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could we -- could you tell us the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Unfortunately it's on -- the photograph page doesn't have a number. If it's placed on the ELMO, and then afterwards I can find the page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's simply to ask you this, whether on that page do you recognise that person and whether that was the surgeon?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that's the man that operated on me. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Nedret Mujkanovic it says there. MR. JONES I'm just reading from the caption for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is shown a photo of a gentleman standing in front of what appears to be a Red Cross ambulance or an ambulance with a Red Cross, anyway, with the words "Dr. Nedret Mujkanovic, after returning to Tuzla from Srebrenica, April 1993."

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm being reminded that the witness should also sign the maps before they're returned to the file.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask you, Captain MacDonald, if you can initial the maps which will be placed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both of them, 905 and 895.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And just two short questions before the break. Firstly, what sort of the job did the surgeon do on you and Tony Birtley?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Considering the lack of proper equipment and a real operating room, I've been told by doctors over the years that a good job had been done on my leg. Although it wasn't the way they would have done it, but I was well taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did he save Tony Birtley's leg in essence?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, he did save Tony Birtley's leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And a third question: Were you eventually air-lifted out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: I was lifted out on the 4th of April, approximately 24 hours after I had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I guess that's a perfect moment for the break. In fact, I anticipate I'll finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. In that case, Mr. Wubben, do you wish to start your cross-examination today or tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Tomorrow, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 30-minute break. We can afford that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Just a few more questions for you this afternoon, Captain MacDonald. Firstly I would ask you to look at a photograph which will be passed up; it's Defence Exhibit D872. If you could look at that, and I'll simply ask you if you recognise the man on the right, the far right of the picture. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yeah, I recognise him. He was the liaison officer that we dealt with, and I had talked with him on a number of occasions. I do not recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say "that we dealt with," does that refer to the -- you and the other UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Do you or do you not know to whom he was reporting, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: No, I never -- that was not part of what I dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I want to ask you a couple more questions about the bombing -- about bombing from planes and use of artillery. As a military man with your training in field artillery, are you familiar with the term "a kill radius"?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what does that refer to and can you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: One artillery round -- to put it down, I guess, to the simplest terms, one artillery round when it lands has a kill radius or what we call a kill zone. And depending on the size of the round, it will have a smaller or bigger kill radius. Any man standing in that circle is highly likely to be killed or wounded. So, for example, 155-millimetre artillery round, a kill radius would be 50 metres. If you fire more than one artillery round from a gun or from a battery of guns, the kill radius is going to be bigger because all the rounds are not going to land in the same hole. So you're going to expand the kill zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And when you say "the rounds are not going to land in the same hole," is that even if they're aiming for the same location, that there will be discrepancies and they'll land in different locations?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Guns have barrel wear after firing a number of rounds plus imperfections in the ammunition plus wind will actually make a round go slightly off course. So that being said you'll never have all the rounds land in the same spot; that's physically impossible to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That example you've given where you have firing from a battery of guns with a larger kill radius, if these guns are firing at different locations, say within a village, will the radius be even greater, the kill radius?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Normally -- normally when you fire a battery of guns you fire on the same grid, but if you fire on different grids, then there's potential for the radius to be bigger.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Say you have a number of heavy-calibre guns firing into a small location, say a small village, would the shrapnel then be spread over the whole area, pretty much indiscriminately?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, that's entirely possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the concept of a denial plan?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: A denial plan in military terms is a plan for denying the use of our equipment or ammunition to the enemy. So if we have to withdraw or if we have to abandon our positions and we have to do it quickly because of enemy pressure, then we would have a plan in place on what we were to destroy in place and how to destroy it. And that's known as a denial plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So that would involve the destruction of your own equipment and/or ammunition to the enemy?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, we would blow up our ammunition that we couldn't carry with us, and equipment would be destroyed so it would be beyond use to the enemy. And obviously we would have to do this quickly because they may be right over the hill and we have to get out of there quick. So based on the amount of time that we would have, we may destroy things more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And is that something unique to the Canadian Armed Forces, or is it standard military practice?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: That would be standard military practice, definitely in NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And finally on this theme, are you familiar with a concept known as FPF or final protective fire?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And can you explain for us what that's about?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: We use final protective fire where we would actually bring -- we would have a target just to the front of our position. And if we were about to be overrun by an enemy force, we could call down fire on that position as a last-ditch effort to try and stop that enemy attack. As an artillery officer, we used to lay our guns on the FPF at night-time and a soldier laying by the gun could fire that in seconds, it was called, to give the infantry soldiers that defensive fire, protective fire. It has to be fired quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And do you know if armies in your experience or to your knowledge have ever practiced calling down final protective fire on their own position?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I've studied some historical examples, even in some of the movies. During the Vietnam war the Americans were known to call fire down on themselves, and that would be the FPF, because they were being overrun by the enemy forces. And if you're down inside your trenches or your bunkers and the enemy is on top of the ground, then there's a good chance you're going to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to review a few more documents with you. The first one is D740, Defence Exhibit D740. And while that's being passed up I'll just read for the record. It's Bratunac garrison command, it's dated 6th of October, 1992, urgent to Birac brigade command. And it says, the second sentence of the second paragraph: "In the enemy attack on Fakovici yesterday," so that would be the 5th of October, 1992, "20 people were killed and one person went missing. The enemy captured two 20-millimetre anti-aircraft guns, a three-barrelled and a four-barrelled one; three 82-millimetre mortars with about 60 shells; an M-84, PM, light machine-gun; two M53-PMs and about ten APM." Now, this describes captured weaponry. Now, in terms of that list and what you see there as it simply as being captured, what, if anything, can you say about the unit which had these weapons?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, it appears to come have an organised unit. These would be typical weapons that you would find in what you call in NATO terms or in Canadian terms as a combined arms team. So I'm looking here and seeing anti-aircraft weapons from an air defence unit, mortars from an artillery or infantry unit, and machine-guns, and I guess the other equipment there. So from a unit that was trained and knew how to use this stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: You've described for us that a battery is I think you said six to eight guns. So three mortars would be half a mortar battery. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yeah, we would call that a group. So that would be probably the minimum that you would use.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the concept of home defence or home guard? Does that concept exist in Canada?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it does today and historically during World War II, although there's a different term that we call it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would a home guard have artillery weapons like those listed here?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that exhibit. I'd just like now if you could look at D469, Defence Exhibit 469. And this is dated 9th of January, 1993, to the Drina Corps command. And I'm going to read for the record. "In the course of combat between the hours of 0830 and 1800 on 7 January, 1993, during the withdrawal of the 3rd Kravica PB infantry battalion, the following MTS was left behind in Kravica." And then we have a list of a number of items, and then it says "destroyed" towards the bottom, B. Now, this document obviously refers specifically to a battalion, the 3rd Kravica Infantry Battalion, and what was left behind in Kravica when that battalion withdrew on the 7th of January, 1993. Now, is it right in light of what you told us earlier or not that it is common military practice for a retreating army to destroy its own weapons if it cannot take them?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, it is, if you have time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And would that include warehouses, for example, where weapons or ammunition are stored to prevent the enemy from capturing them?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Certainly there would be a plan for all equipment, even in a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, this list refers to a three-barrelled gun, four-barrelled gun, ZIS gun, six mortars, anti-aircraft guns. Again, is this weapons of a properly equipped battalion or is it something which would belong to a home guard or a village guard?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: This is consistent, what you would find in an infantry battalion or a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And according to this list, this is simply what was captured or destroyed, not necessarily all the weaponry in Kravica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, so far it has some line in it. The line is that witness is now already for some time requested his observations but also his opinion in comparing a Canadian army/NATO army situation with another situation in Bosnia. And that situation he didn't saw by himself, he didn't monitor it by himself. It has been put to him through this -- through my learned friend. Well, there comes a time -- it is a grey line when it comes from a witness a step over to become a kind of expert, and I think now the time has come to make objections. When my learned friend put to him the content of letters, orders, or whatsoever, and asked his conclusions to compare it with similar situations and like an expert would do. And I protest against it. It's all about a witness for fact-finding and such has been presented to us also via the summary and not as an expert, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I simply don't understand the objection because my question was: "According to this list, this is simply what was captured or destroyed, not necessarily all the weaponry, in Kravica?" That's simply a comment on what's on the face of the document. In fact, I don't even really need to put the question because the document speaks for itself. If Mr. Wubben is now belatedly, I emphasise belatedly, making a point about questions which were asked earlier, then he's simply too late. It's a basic principle that a party has to object in a timely fashion. And so as far as that objection is to my last question, I submit I have no application whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last question, ignore it completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right, so it is a belated reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The substance of his objection obviously does not really tie-up with your last question. It ties up with --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's why I say, Your Honour, objections have to be timely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But apart from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And secondly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is another issue involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Of course, but it's an important point, Your Honour. It's not open to any party to object to a question that was asked two hours ago. But secondly, the witness has answered questions that are entirely in his knowledge. He is a field artillery officer. He has not been giving opinions; he's been stating what the practice is, not just in Canada but is practise in armed forces generally, and he's been also referring to what he observed, I don't know how far I have to go back now in his evidence, but he's referred to what he saw with his own eyes, guns firing, effect of guns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop because we have got the witness present and I would rather conclude on this very quickly. Mr. Wubben, your last comments on this and I will confer with my two colleagues and decide on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's not only what this witness observed, not only questions to what the practice is in Canada, it's not limited to those issues, it's also making conclusions upon suggestions by this counsel, and that's my protest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So very simply put, Mr. Wubben and Mr. Jones, the position as we see it is that we don't read in your questions an attempt to try and elicit expert advice from the witness. That's number one. Number two, any testimony that he may have given, that he has actually given based on his knowledge and comparative knowledge with the Canadian army or NATO or military doctrine and strategy in general, we do not take it that he has tried to answer as an expert. And any question that you feel uncomfortable about, you can deal with on cross-examination. If he has testified on the situation as it obtains in Canada or whatever, you can ask him whether he is in a position to know or to inform us what was the position or if he is aware of what the practice and position was in the former Yugoslavia, and that's it. If he knows, he will answer; if he doesn't, the situation will remain as it is. He has testified on the practice in Canada and in NATO countries. We don't really see the substance of the objection, and we are not taking the witness as a witness testifying basically on -- as an expert. He is testifying -- he is being asked questions which he is answering based on his knowledge and experience. And we are taking it as that. I mean, he can be confuted and challenged with any question on cross-examination on that. All right. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Jones, you've got 15 minutes to conclude, otherwise we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. May I just say I take Your Honour's point. Simply, the reason I insist so much is on a timely objection is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Because otherwise I ask questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. I didn't touch on it because it is obvious. Once it has passed, it has passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Now, finally, just turning back to your report and in fact you don't necessarily need it in front of you, but it's the line five -- sentence five lines from the bottom. "One year in a combat zone is definitely enough for the time being." I just want to focus on that in relation to a time in Srebrenica. Was there a plan among the UNMOs for rotation every week or so because of the traumas of being in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. Initially when we were -- when we went into Srebrenica they told us that we would need to be equipped for 15 days. And then immediately a plan that we would rotate half the team every Friday, so once a week. However, this didn't necessarily happen but I have no information on how it worked because I was Med-Evac'ed out of there on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that plan?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Well, the conditions were so bad. We were eating rations, we didn't have clean drinking water. I had actually gotten sick probably from the sanitary and -- sanitary conditions and the bad water and the high stress. It was a very stressful time. So you would try to rotate people out so they would get the experience and you could basically de-stress back in a less stressful location.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that even hardened UNMOs were suffering trauma after even a very brief periods in the enclave, due to the conditions there?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, we had to deal with the same situation as the local population, and in some cases even more due to the job that we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And did you come across, and you don't need to mention any names, but UNMOs who suffered severe post-traumatic stress as a result of witnesses events in the Konjevic Polje-Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Sometimes a critical incident can affect you immediately to your detriment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For Bosnian fighters who were there for years, what would the trauma have been like?

utterances.speaker: DAVE MacDONALD
utterances.text: Everybody deals with trauma differently and some people can handle it and it won't necessarily affect them, and others, like I said, one simple event can -- they can snap.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So -- before we quit for the day you will recall about two months ago I had mentioned to you the possibility of sitting down together and trying to agree on a document which would be made available to the Trial Chamber describing -- naming and describing the various kinds of weapons. Did you do anything about it? I suppose you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's been an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: There has been an exchange so far and we made some suggestions. The response by my learned friends was that they are on the review of various definitions. The Defence had, for themselves, also a suggestion, meaning a kind of overview. So we are definitely working on it. It should be something that comes out of both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I wanted to make sure that you have not shelved it or put it in deep freeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It would become very useful because it will ensure some kind of uniformity on the part of the Chamber when approaching the armament issue. All right? Thank you. Captain, we will stop here for today. I take it, Mr. Wubben - and I won't be too optimistic in expecting that you would probably finish your cross-examination tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So tomorrow your ordeal will be over, Captain, and you will be able to return back home. So I thank you so much. You will now be escorted by Madam Usher. In the meantime, between today and tomorrow, be sure that you don't communicate or let anyone communicate with you on the matters related to your testimony or to the subject matter of this case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of November, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
